description.short: A light, floral Anxi oolong often appreciated as an accessible sister variety to Tie Guan Yin
description.overview: Grown alongside Tie Guan Yin across the terroirs of Anxi County and processed in a similar fashion, but crafted from a distinct, hardier, and higher-yielding cultivar.
description.leaf: Tightly rolled light-green pearls, visually almost indistinguishable from Tie Guan Yin
description.aroma: Floral, slightly lighter and softer than Tie Guan Yin
description.taste: Smooth, floral, with a lighter body and gentle sweetness
description.processing: Follows the general Anxi ball-rolled oolong technique: withering → shaking/tossing → fixation (kill-green) → cloth-wrapped rolling into balls → light drying

history.origin: The name means 'Source Mountain' or 'Native Mountain' (Ben Shan), emphasizing that this cultivar is native to the same heartland as Tie Guan Yin.
history.development: Historically cultivated as an easier-to-grow, resilient, and more productive alternative to Tie Guan Yin across Anxi family farms.
history.modern: Due to its striking visual similarity to Tie Guan Yin, it has sometimes been substituted for it; connoisseurs distinguish it in the cup by its lighter body and more delicate, straightforward floral fragrance.
interestingFacts: Ben Shan and Tie Guan Yin look so similar as dry rolled leaf that they are virtually identical to the naked eye; the distinction reveals itself in the brewed cup.
Ben Shan's vigor, disease resistance, and reliable yield made it historically essential for the livelihood of Anxi tea-farming communities.
